# Judges Chapter 21 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), c. 1008 CE | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JDG_page_291.jpg, JDG_page_292.jpg

1. Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "No one of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin."

2. And the people came to Bethel and sat there till evening before God, and they lifted up their voices and wept bitterly.

3. And they said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?"

4. And on the next day the people rose early and built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

5. And the people of Israel said, "Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, "He shall surely be put to death."

6. And the people of Israel had compassion for Benjamin their brother and said, "One tribe is cut off from Israel this day.

7. "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?"

8. And they said, "What one is there of the tribes of Israel that did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah?" And behold, no one had come to the camp from Jabesh-gilead, to the assembly.

9. For when the people were mustered, behold, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there.

10. So the congregation sent 12,000 of their bravest men there and commanded them, "Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword; also the women and the little ones.

11. "This is what you shall do: every male and every woman that has lain with a male you shall devote to destruction."

12. And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead 400 young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.

13. Then the whole congregation sent word to the people of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them.

14. And Benjamin returned at that time. And they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh-gilead, but they were not enough for them.

15. And the people had compassion on Benjamin because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.

16. Then the elders of the congregation said, "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?"

17. And they said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, that a tribe may not be blotted out from Israel.

18. "Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the people of Israel had sworn, "Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin."

19. So they said, "Behold, there is the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."

20. And they commanded the people of Benjamin, "Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards

21. "and watch. If the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and each of you seize his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

22. "And when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Grant them graciously to us, because we did not take for each man of them his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, else you would now be guilty.'"

23. And the people of Benjamin did so and took their wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went and returned to their inheritance and rebuilt the cities and lived in them.

24. And the people of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and his clan, and they went out from there every man to his inheritance.

25. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 21 is the book's coda — the aftermath of civil war. Having nearly annihilated Benjamin, Israel now scrambles to preserve it. The solutions are progressively more desperate and morally bankrupt: first the destruction of Jabesh-gilead to procure wives (another cherem against fellow Israelites), then the engineered abduction of women at Shiloh's festival. The book that began with Israel asking God "Who shall go up?" ends with Israel engineering kidnappings at a religious festival.

The final verse — "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" — is simultaneously a diagnosis, a verdict, and an implicit plea. The word "right" (yashar) runs through the book like a thread: Samson saw what was "right in his eyes" (14:3); now all Israel does the same. The book's thesis is not that people did evil — many thought they were doing good — but that moral autonomy without covenant authority produces atrocity dressed as righteousness.

The four-fold refrain (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25) structures the appendix and, retrospectively, the entire book. It points forward to the monarchy narratives (1-2 Samuel), where the "king" solution will be tested — and found wanting in its own way.

---
## ⚠️ Disagreement Log

### v.25 — "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" vs. "everyone did as they saw fit"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Each man did the right in his own eyes" | ish hayyashar b'einav ya'aseh — literal |
| LOGOS | "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" | Same, smoother English |
| PNEUMA | "everyone did as they saw fit" | Dynamic — drops "right" and "eyes" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. This is the book's final word — the climactic occurrence of the four-fold refrain (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). As argued at 17:6, the word "right" (yashar) is the theological crux: the problem is not anarchy but moral autonomy masquerading as righteousness. PNEUMA's "as they saw fit" describes behavioral freedom; LOGOS's "what was right in his own eyes" describes the corruption of moral judgment itself. At the book's conclusion, this distinction matters supremely.

**Status:** Critical. The book's final word and thesis statement — must preserve "right in his own eyes."

---

### v.11 — "devote to destruction" vs. "kill" vs. "destroy completely"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "you shall devote to destruction" | tacharim — from cherem, holy-war vocabulary |
| LOGOS | "you shall devote to destruction" | Same — preserves cherem echo |
| PNEUMA | "kill" | Simplifies, loses cherem language |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The verb tacharim (from cherem) is holy-war vocabulary — the same word used for the destruction of Canaanite cities (Deut 7:2; Josh 6:21). Its use here, against fellow Israelites at Jabesh-gilead, is the chapter's most devastating irony: Israel applies to its own people the destruction reserved for God's enemies. PNEUMA's "kill" is accurate but loses the theological echo entirely.

**Status:** Major. Cherem vocabulary — connects to Joshua's conquest and chapter 20's destruction of Benjamin.

---

### v.21 — "seize" vs. "grab" vs. "take"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "seize" | chataf — to snatch, grab by force |
| LOGOS | "seize" | Same |
| PNEUMA | "grab" | Colloquial synonym |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew chataf means "to snatch, seize by force." Both "seize" and "grab" convey the violence, but "seize" has the appropriate register for a narrative that documents the calculated abduction of women at a religious festival. "Grab" is too casual for the gravity of the act.

**Status:** Minor. Register choice.

---

### v.22 — "Grant them graciously to us" vs. "Do them a favor for our sake"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Be gracious to them for our sake" | chonnu otam — from chanan, "to be gracious" |
| LOGOS | "Grant them graciously to us" | Formal rendering of chanan |
| PNEUMA | "Do them a favor for our sake" | Dynamic, loses "gracious" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The verb chanan ("to be gracious/grant favor") is used in prayer language throughout the OT (cf. Ps 4:1; 6:2; 51:1). Its use here — in the mouths of elders engineering an abduction — is deeply ironic. They ask for "grace" to justify kidnapping. PNEUMA's "do them a favor" captures the social transaction but loses the prayer-language irony.

**Status:** Moderate. Ironic use of prayer vocabulary in a morally bankrupt context.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Book thesis statement | 1 | "Right in his own eyes" — the book's final word (v.25) |
| Cherem vocabulary | 1 | Holy-war language against fellow Israelites (v.11) |
| Register in violent context | 1 | chataf — "seize" vs. "grab" (v.21) |
| Ironic prayer language | 1 | chanan — "be gracious" in abduction context (v.22) |

**Overall pattern:** The critical disagreement is again v.25 — the book's thesis statement in its final, climactic occurrence. PNEUMA's consistent rendering ("as they saw fit") strips the refrain of its theological core throughout chapters 17-21. The secondary disagreement is v.11's cherem vocabulary, which connects Jabesh-gilead's destruction to the conquest narratives and to chapter 20's destruction of Benjamin — a chain of holy-war language applied inward that charts Israel's complete moral inversion.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
